claims.text: The target material is a noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticle containing more than five elements.
The precursor components initially have a heterogeneous spatial distribution.
Introducing a controlled dwell at peak temperature extends the time available for atomic diffusion before cooling.
A short dwell at peak temperature permits sufficient atomic interdiffusion to homogenize the precursor mixture.
Greater atomic interdiffusion produces greater local elemental homogeneity before nucleation.
High temperature increases atomic mobility and thereby enhances interdiffusion.
Elemental uniformity facilitates nucleation of a single-phase solid solution.
Insufficient diffusion time during ultrafast heating preserves compositional inhomogeneities.
Rapid cooling freezes local compositional inhomogeneities into the nanoparticles.
Frozen compositional inhomogeneities lead to phase separation and elemental segregation.
Frozen compositional inhomogeneities lead to irregular particle morphologies.
An optimally extended dwell will yield a more uniform, single-phase solid solution with less elemental segregation than a negligible-dwell baseline.
Rapid heating and cooling with little or no peak-temperature dwell produces observable phase separation and elemental segregation.
There is a synthesis-temperature window suitable for forming a single high-entropy phase.
Excessively long dwell times may allow conventional diffusion or coarsening to dominate.
Temperatures outside the effective-mobility window may fail to homogenize the material or may trigger decomposition.
The optimal dwell time and temperature window depend on noble-metal composition and particle size.

contradictions.description: The boundary anticipates that sufficiently long dwell times may cause coarsening or other competing behavior, but the falsification rule treats increased phase separation at an extended dwell as falsifying the mechanism. Without defining the admissible dwell-time range, an outcome attributed to the stated boundary could also be labeled falsification.

The prediction invokes an optimal dwell time, implying potentially nonmonotonic behavior, whereas the falsification rule asks for systematic improvement as dwell time increases. Improvement up to an optimum followed by deterioration would satisfy the prediction but could fail the stated rule.
